(1) B. mycoids strains are able to form rhizoid colonies, but not all strains of the species do; (2) the species can be identified by fatty acid analysis, 16S rRNA sequence analysis and species-specific oligonucleotide probes; and (3) the 16S sequence analysis and species specific oligonucleotide hybridization confirmed the close relatedness between B. mycroides and B. cereus and B. thuringensis.
the 16S-rDNA probe is a valuable tool for the identification of B. mycoide s, and that B. mycoids strains isolated from peat bogs are phenotypically different from the type strain.
fatty acid analysis and 16S rRNA gene sequence analysis can be used to identify B. mycoids strains and that the 16S gene sequence analysis can discriminate B. mycoide from other Bacillus species.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification and characterization of B. myocoides strains isolated from an extreme environment, and provides evidence for the existence of a new subspecies of B. mycocoides.

the identification of environmental strains of B. cereus group species by fatty acid analysis, 16S rRNA analysis and species-specific DNA probes and the development of a new species-specific 16SrDNA oligonucleotid probe for the identification of B. mycoide strains.

the identification of B. mycoides strains from a peat environment by fatty acid analysis, 16S rRNA gene analysis and DNA-Dna hybridization and the design of a species-specific 16 S rRNA gene probe for the identification of these strains.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the strains of the present study are environmental isolates of B. mycoides, which differ from the type strain by their motility and rhizoid colony formation.
the strains isolated from peat bog are environmental isolates of B. myooides.
B. mycoids, B. cereuses, B. thurigenisis and B. anthraxis are closely related species and that the type strains of these species are very similar, but not identical.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the 16S ribosomal RNA gene is a good marker for the identification of B. mycoide strains and that fatty acid analysis is a good marker to identify B. cereus and related species.

the type strains of these species, as well as the environmental strains of B. thuringensis and B. anthraceis, are clearly distinguishable by their fatty acid composition and by their 16S rRNA sequences.
B. mycoids is the only species of the B. cereus group that can be identified by 16S ribosomal DNA analysis and by a 16S ribosome probe.
The main takeaway from our work is that
B. mycoids is a heterogeneous species that is comprised of at least three distinct subgroups.
